“Jobs are back” sounds like a finish line. But a national total can recover
while particular industries still employ fewer people. **When U.S. payroll
employment regained its February 2020 level, had every major sector recovered
too?** That distinction matters when judging what a recovery headline tells
someone looking for work in a particular part of the economy.

The answer is no. In this data snapshot, total nonfarm payrolls first returned
to their starting level in **`r month_text`**, yet **`r below_return` of the
eleven major sectors** remained below theirs. The interactive chart lets you
inspect those differences rather than treating the national line as everyone's
experience.

## Explore the recovery

The data are monthly, seasonally adjusted estimates from the [Bureau of Labor
Statistics payroll survey](https://www.bls.gov/ces/), obtained through
[FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PAYEMS). The chart follows February
2020 through December 2024, using eleven broad sectors, including government,
alongside the national total. Each percentage line starts at zero because it
compares a sector with its own February 2020 payroll count. Seasonal adjustment
reduces recurring calendar effects, making month-to-month comparisons more useful.

**Try this:** hover or tap a line for its date, payroll count, and both measures
of change. Click legend entries to show or hide sectors; double-click one to
isolate it. The dropdown restores the recovery comparison, selects
goods-producing sectors, or displays every sector. Switch between **% change**
and **Job change**; the latter axis is in thousands. Drag the date slider to
inspect a shorter period, or drag a box within the plot to zoom. Double-click
the plot to reset the zoom.


## A national crossing, several unfinished recoveries

Start with the default comparison and hover around the vertical line.
Professional and business services stood **`r pct_text(at_return("USPBS", "change_pct"))`
above** its starting level. Leisure and hospitality was still
**`r pct_text(at_return("USLAH", "change_pct"))` below**, representing
**`r jobs_text(at_return("USLAH", "change_thousands"))` fewer jobs**. Private
education and health services, other services, mining and logging, and
government were also below baseline. Gains elsewhere were sufficient to offset
these remaining shortfalls in the national total.

This is why a recovery date needs a clearly defined unit. It marks when a
total crosses a threshold; it does not establish that the same workers found
new jobs, that vacancies were plentiful, or that wages recovered. Payroll
statistics count jobs rather than unique people: someone holding two payroll
jobs can be counted twice, as [BLS
explains](https://www.bls.gov/bls/empsitquickguide.htm).

## The units change the comparison

Now compare mining and logging with private education and health services
near the end of 2024. Mining was **`r pct_text(at_end("USMINE", "change_pct"))`
below** baseline, while private education and health was
**`r pct_text(at_end("USEHS", "change_pct"))` above**. Those percentages have
similar magnitudes. Switching to **Job change** reveals very different scales:
about **`r jobs_text(at_end("USMINE", "change_thousands"))` jobs lost** versus
**`r jobs_text(at_end("USEHS", "change_thousands"))` gained**. Percentage changes
describe the size of a shift relative to a sector; job counts describe its
numerical contribution to the national change. Neither answers both questions.

Select **Goods-producing sectors** and follow manufacturing after its first
return above zero. By December 2024 it was slightly below baseline again.
Returning once is not the same as remaining above the threshold. Across all
sectors, **`r below_end`** ended the window below baseline, although **`r small_gaps`** of
those gaps were less than one percent. These small endpoint differences should
not be described as evidence of a large collapse.

These are revised historical estimates downloaded in 2026, not the numbers
available to journalists in 2022. [BLS revises payroll
estimates](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesvininfo.htm), so crossing dates can
change. The chart does not identify why sectors diverged, and returning to
2020 employment is not equivalent to catching up with population growth or a
pre-pandemic trend. **The takeaway: the national total recovered before every
sector did. Check the sector, date, and units before interpreting what “jobs
are back” means.**
